title: How Karma Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the concept of karma across Eastern religions and its adoption in the West. They cover Hinduism (samsara, moksha, three types of karma: prarabdha, sanchita, agami), Buddhism (karma as the link between lives, the "germ of consciousness" or vijnana, Buddha's "heirs of our own actions," asana or deathbed karma), Sikhism (fate as a river with free will as waves, God can create or destroy karma), and Jainism (karma as a physical substance attaching to the jiva, eight main types and 158 subtypes, dust-brooms). They then discuss Western karma as a pop-culture buzzword, tracing its introduction to Helena Blavatsky and the Theosophical Society, the Age of Aquarius, and John Lennon's "Instant Karma." The episode closes with a listener mail segment about John Billington descendants and a "karma off" call for listener stories.

segments.title: Opening banter and karma in pop culture
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with off-topic chat about a carbonated beverage and then discuss how people invoke karma after the Casey Anthony verdict, contrasting popular Western usage with the traditional view of karma as negative.

segments.title: Karma origins and Eastern traditions overview
segments.summary: They note the Sanskrit and Pali roots of karma meaning act, and list the four Eastern religions that believe in karma: Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, and Jainism.

segments.title: Karma in Hinduism
segments.summary: Karma keeps souls in samsara, the cycle of rebirth, until moksha is reached. Karma clings to the soul and is independent of the gods. Good karma comes from fulfilling caste duties. Three types are described: prarabdha, sanchita, and agami.

segments.title: Karma in Buddhism
segments.summary: Buddhists have no soul as Westerners understand it; karma links one life to the next and forms the germ of consciousness (vijnana). Buddha taught that people are heirs of their own actions and rejected strict fatalism. Vipaka is the result of karma, and asana is deathbed karma with outsized weight.

segments.title: Karma in Sikhism
segments.summary: Sikh karma is the accumulation of past deeds' effects on character, which survives death. Dr. Gobind Singh Mansukhani describes fate as a river in which human actions make waves, and says God can create or destroy karma through good deeds and prayer.

segments.title: Karma in Jainism
segments.summary: Jains consider karma a physical substance of particles attracted to the soul by thoughts, words, and deeds, binding it to rebirth. They classify karma into eight main types and 158 subtypes, and practice ascetic living such as sweeping before sitting to avoid harming life.

segments.title: Western karma and Helena Blavatsky
segments.summary: Western karma is a buzzword, often used as tipping or wishing bad luck on others. The concept was introduced to the West by Helena Blavatsky, who co-founded the Theosophical Society with Henry Steele Olcott. Her ideas were tied to the Age of Aquarius. John Lennon's 'Instant Karma' is mentioned.

segments.title: Closing reflections on karma
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck share personal views: doing good is right regardless of cosmic law, and good deeds open one up to noticing goodness in others.

segments.title: Listener mail on John Billington and karma off
segments.summary: A listener from Elburn, Illinois, writes about being related to John Billington and enjoying the First Murderer episode. The hosts then invite listeners to submit good-karma stories for an unofficial 'karma off'.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give contact information for submissions and promote the Stuff from the Future video podcast before signing off.
